I can share some pains, design decisions and experiences we had with relative references over the years. This is from my work with [Unpoly](https://unpoly.com/), an HTML extension where [links update fragments](https://unpoly.com/up.link) instead of full pages. For this we needed a way to reliably target elements.

- We use CSS selectors to [target fragments](https://unpoly.com/targeting-fragments). We haven't had a need for something more powerful since `:has()`.
- We also use a pseudo `:origin` to refer to the current element (`:scope` wasn't a thing when we named this).
- When you show content in overlays ("dialog", "modal"), the risk of references matching the wrong element increases. In Unpoly CSS selectors never match an element in another layer unless the other explicitly allows this with an `[up-layer=any]` attribute. I feel this is already an issue in HTML since `<dialog>` was introduced.
- A sharp edge with `<label for="some-id">` is that clicking will blindly focus the first element with that `id`. Unintuitvely this may match elements in another form, or in another layer. We patch the `label` / `input` matching so elements within the same form are preferred.
- A very common use case is to match within an ancestor of the current element. E.g. the form of an input, or another input within the same form. You can do this explicitly `:has()` and `:origin`, e.g. `form:has(:origin) .other-input`.
- For convenience we also match ancestor elements preferrably. E.g. `form` would first look for the closest ancestor `form` and only then look through the rest of the page. Also `form .other-input` would first try to find `.other-input` within the same form, before looking at other forms.

We have not needed introduce new syntax aside from `:origin` and `:has()` (before browser support was there). However, a similiar library [htmx](https://htmx.org/) uses [custom selector synxtax](https://htmx.org/attributes/hx-target/) like `closest .foo`.

This is another area where it makes it hard to reason about server side template partials like I discussed re `hN` tags in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5033#issuecomment-547138261

Another problem with `id` other than uniqueness is that it does way too much.

I would like something like this sketch:

A `refscope` tag (or maybe it's an attribute) defines a new scope. `:root` implicitly defines a root scope.

Elements have a `ref` attr to use instead of `id`. Unlike `id` it only defines a name and that name is local to the current scope. (If there are multiple identically named refs, then which one wins should be defined in the standard and browsers should print a warning in the debug console.)

If something is referred to by name, the refs in the current scope are searched first. If there's no match, check the parent scope; repeating as necessary until reaching the root scope. If there's no match after all that, check for a matching `id`.

A tag could have both a `ref` and `id` and that may be confusing and certainly not recommended but everything works out.

The MathML 4 effort has some overlapping interest in improved DX for referencing. Exactly due to the difficulties of managing global ids, we have tentatively introduced a new `arg` attribute to anchor referencing in MathML Intent, targeting the feature of accessible navigation of math expressions:
https://w3c.github.io/mathml/spec.html#intent_reference

Simple example:
```html
<msup intent="power($base,$exp)">
  <mi arg="base">x</mi>
  <mi arg="exp">n</mi>
</msup>
```

We have had the constraint of keeping the traversal algorithm as simple as possible, which has so far kept us from introducing relative selectors (sibling, ancestor). Nevertheless, MathML has viable use cases where relative selectors are quite natural, such as accessible walks through tabular diagrams (realized via `<mtable>`).

The traversal algorithm for `intent`/`arg` referencing is scoped to the current subtree (references can only point to descendant nodes). It also has an additional stopping condition at nodes carrying the `intent` or `arg` attributes, to allow stacking of multiple math notations.

As we have multi-format content (such as scientific diagrams via SVG+MathML, as well as block equations mixed with text), it would be a significant boost to DX if we could share a uniform referencing scheme.

The reasons I think XPath may be worth considering here are:

1. XPath already has solid syntax for relative paths starting from somewhere in the middle of a tree
2. I think CSS selectors and XPath are optimized for slightly different problems:

Both XPath and Selectors do the same thing, just with slightly different powers due to historical circumstance. XPath is a little stronger on crawling the tree, Selectors is a little stronger on querying individual elements. That's it; they're otherwise identical technologies at a slightly abstract level.

The downside of using XPath is that it's a second querying language, *similar to* but *different from* Selectors, and their behavior and functionality largely overlap. The Web already contains a profusion of languages, and we should be careful with adding more. (Yes, XPath is technically exposed via one DOM method already, but it's little-known.) It also means the large variety of element qualities that Selectors can match on wouldn't be available; we'd be restricted to the much more limited set of things XPath can inspect.

The downside of using Selectors is that we might need to add more combinators to handle traversing along additional axises beyond just "descendants" and "following siblings", and these wouldn't be valid in CSS for perf reasons. But we have the theoretical structure for this (`/foo(...)/` combinators), so maybe it wouldn't be too bad.

A "closest ancestor" mechanism is meaningfully different from `section:has(&)` when you nest similar components. The latter will select *both* the nearest section *and* a further ancestor section, allowing the rest of the selector to potentially match in the outer component instead. Finding a "closest" one instead avoids this issue. It's very important to make it easy to correctly catch the intended "upper scoping boundary"  (and a lower scoping boundary, too).

In other words, I think this'll need something like our [`@scope` selectors](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-cascade-6/#scope-syntax) to (optionally) establish bounds, followed by the actual selector.

Since we'll likely also need an introductory prefix to syntactically mark this as distinct from an IDREF, I'm going to assume for a moment that `@` will work, as that's unlikely to have ever been used at scale to start IDs. This also lets us lean more into CSS, as I'll explore in my example.

So, I'm imagining something like `for="@ .foo"` for the simplest cases, just finding the (first in DOM order?) element on the page with the `.foo` class. (`for="foo"` would be equivalent to `for="@ #foo"`.) For Noam's most recent example, something like `for="@scope (section) form input[name=myfield]"`. The `section` upper-bound scoping selector find the *nearest ancestor* to the element in question (a `label`, in this case) that matches the selector.

We designed `@scope`'s syntax well here, in parenthesizing both of its selector arguments, so we have some relatively unambiguous grammar here, so we can do lower bounds too, like `for="@scope (.media-object) to (.content > *) input[name=myfield]"` to limit the search to only within the bounds of the "media object" component, not its (arbitrary) contents.

This sort of syntax isn't workable in a selector. You're attempting to apply some *context* to change how the `input` part of the selector matches, but you're doing so via pseudo-classes (which just filter the result set) on a preceding compound selector (which is selecting some ancestor of the `input` element).

That's the big issue with trying to put these semantics into Selectors proper - a "closest" bound is, if anything, a *combinator*, but a complicated one. And lower bounds can't be done in existing Selector mechanics at all; they need to change the context of how you match the thing "between" the bounds. That's why we have `@scope` in CSS as an at-rule that takes the upper/lower bound selectors separately, and changes the mechanics of how its contained rules match, rather than trying to do this by just adding to Selectors itself.

> `&:closest(.media-object) button` feels already natural to me, consistent with the existing `Element.closest`,

Similarly, this doesn't work. Pseudo-classes are simple selectors, and thus can only filter the existing result set - starting from `&` (the element itself), all it can do is leave you with that element, or reduce it to the empty set. You want a *combinator*, which is how we change the matched set to other related elements. However, it's not a simple combinator that transforms the set via a static relationship, it needs to take an argument itself. (You can't just rely on the following compound selector, like `& /closest-ancestor/ .media-object`, because that opens up ambiguity if the upper-bound selector is, itself, complex (containing a combinator).

But as I just stated above, you can't solve the lower bound problem in the same way, in any case, because it changes how a *different* part of the selector matches.

If done directly in Selectors, then, we'd be reduced to smuggling all of it into a few all-consuming pseudo-classes anyway, like: `:closest(.media-object, &) input:not-in(.content > *)`. And that's *still* wrong, in fact, because the lower-bound selector needs to be aware of the upper bound selector so it only matches and excludes subtrees that start below the upper bound. (Otherwise, nesting media-objects would cause the lower bound to trigger for *all* the elements of the inner object.) 

So really we'd need to do `input:scope(.media-object, .content > *, &)`, just cramming the entire functionality into a pseudoclass so they can all interact as needed. That's pretty unreadable, imo! (It also makes the scoping functionality *much* more powerful than what already exists in `@scope`, since it could apply per compound selector in the selector, which might be a significant departure from how scoped selectors are already stored and evaluated in browsers.

And, again, this isn't the full set of new powers we want. Adding arbitrary shadow piercing is something that was *actively blocked* by implementers in the past, both for implementation reasons and design reasons. Doing cross-shadow-tree matching in *generic* Selectors can be a huge issue for multiple reasons, which don't apply (or at least, don't apply as strongly, or in the same way) for single-shot use-cases like this. So we're going to have to carve out a new microsyntax *anyway*.

> but I think the order should be `.media-object:closest-to(&)`

This one doesn't work either. :( Pseudo-classes can't depend on their order within a compound selector - `:a:b` and `:b:a` have to result in exactly the same result set. And they can't depend contextually on other selectors in the compound, for similar reasons, plus circularity concerns (if in `:a:b` `:a` depends on the rest of the selector (`:b`), but `:b` also depends on the rest of the selector (`:a`), that's circular) - `:a:b` needs to be *precisely* the intersection of what's matched by `:a` and what's matched by `:b`, independently.

The only way to satisfy this is to move both the selector for the target element and the upper bound element into a single pseudo-selector, where you *can* have interaction between them in a well-defined manner. And the same applies to the lower bound. So this brings me back to "just put the whole thing into a single pseudo-class", looking like `input:scope(.media-object, .content > *, &)`, which is bad.

(There's also some complexity/ambiguity around having the "starter" element, from which the upper and lower bounds are derived, being defined by a selector which can match multiple (perhaps nested) elements. Probably not unsolvable, but not trivial. These are side-stepped entirely in the model we're *actually* trying to solve, where the starter element is a single well-known element.)

In the interest of moving this forwards, I'll summarize the current state and any TBDs.

It seems to me that we have consensus that the **problem** needs solving, and that (a subset of) CSS selectors in some shape or form is the right solution.

## Open questions

### 1. What subset of CSS selectors is supported?

In the call today there are some concerns around performance. Ids are highly optimized, whereas selectors less so.
OTOH these are typically not references that change frequently, and matched selectors are already tracked for CSS.

If the entire selector space is deemed a no-go for performance reasons, one solution is to scope this down to a subset of selectors, and expand it as use cases come up. Even with a very restricted set, there is value in using selectors over a custom microsyntax, since there is an obvious path to expansion as needs arise, whereas with a custom microsyntax every use case requires inventing more microsyntax, and eventually developing a parallel selectors language.

One question is whether any pseudo-elements would be allowed, and which ones if so. It seems there is a strong case for element-backed pseudo elements (e.g. `::part()` and `::slotted()`), and a somewhat weaker case for many others.

### 2. Do we introduce new attributes or re-use the same ones through some kind of syntactic switch?

1. If we think reusing existing attributes is otherwise a good path, we need web compat research to see what syntax might be safe for overloading existing attributes
2. If we think introducing _new_ attributes is a better API _anyway_ then no additional compat research is needed. My worry with this is that if we implement this as a prefix or suffix over existing attributes, we will end up with comically long attribute names. But perhaps there exists a prefix or suffix that is sufficiently short that this won't be the case. One advantage of this is that it will not restrict the syntax space at all, whereas with the first option, at the very least type selectors would need to be rewritten (e.g. `foo` instead of `:is(foo)`)
3. Another option is to decouple the "switch" into a different, inherited attribute. Though that would be problematic with the kind of mixing and matching HTML that often happens in real-world cases.

### 3. How to specify the matching scope?

Options discussed:
1. Microsyntax based on CSS `@scope`
2. Separate attribute for setting scope using a selector with `.closest()` semantics
3. Separate boolean attribute for setting scope that goes on the scoping element. Simpler, but it means there cannot be different scopes per use. Though that means it cannot vary on a case by case basis. I can easily imagine authors wanting e.g. to target popovers, dialogs, or datalists that are body children, but use a much narrower scope for linking form controls with their labels.

### 4. What should the default scope be? 

It looks like we have consensus that it should be the whole document (or shadow tree), but may be good to resolve.

Some thoughts & suggestions about which order to tackle these in to move this forwards:

- While this may end up addressing some of the Reference Target use cases, it is ultimately orthogonal to it. If RT is used to redirect references to the host element, that should still work regardless of how the host element was targeted.
- Whatever we come up with, we need to ensure there is a set of APIs that web components authors can use to implement their own reference attributes. E.g. perhaps some sort of observer to monitor matched elements (which is useful *in general*). Though this can ship later.
- 1 seems to be the most important, as it determines whether this is viable at all and also informs the priorities for some of the other questions. E.g. if the set of selectors is highly restricted, being able to specify a scope becomes much more important. 
- After that, I suggest we tackle 2 (syntax) and 4 (default scope) and punt 3 (syntax to customize scope) for later. I've discussed this at length with my community of frontend developers. 
One big issue around IDs is composition. UIs today are often built from a mix and match of components, not all of which use or can use shadow DOM. To work with IDs, all the parties involved in the composition need to agree on a global namespace, or somehow share UUIDs or other very long IDs like some URL scheme.
This often breaks, e.g. with SVG minifiers that shorten your IDs, or if two exported components step on each other's toes.

This is relevant to aria but it is not aria-specific - it's for any feature that uses IDREFs.

In other words, I think the OP identifies the problems well, and the survey results are ample validation.

The downsides of the status quo which have been mentioned are (please comment on any I missed):
1. The global namespace for IDs.
   - This creates a coordination problem which, as @noamr points out, requires all parties involved to agree to some kind of ID scheme to avoid collisions. If the whole page is built with one tool, the tool typically provides such a scheme, but that's not always possible.
2. The necessity of setting matching string values on _two different elements_ in order to create a connection.
   - This is related to the coordination problem and shares tooling solutions with it, but it's also a distinct issue.
3. For accessibility-related attributes in particular, breakages are often obscure to developers.
4. References across shadow root boundaries are not always possible.
   - As far as I know, `referenceTarget` is the only serious proposal for any API which allows cross-shadow root references to be made declaratively, and it is intentionally narrow in scope and only allows references in to shadow roots.
   - Imperative references can be made out of shadow roots, but these aren't serializable.

The OP seems to propose that relative references are the only (or at least best) possible solution to (the first two of) those issues, but I'm not sure I agree with that either.

Since this came up in accessibility-related channels, I thought I might jump in with some of my experiences. My perspective comes from working on multiple component libraries in an accessibility-focused role, and dealing with `id` associations in reusable components for other engineering teams is something I've had to deal with regularly for over a decade, at the expense of my sanity.

Here's an attempt to boil down the relevant constraints and design considerations around creating `id`-based element associations:

- Generally, when creating an `id` association my intent is to use an `id` identify exactly one other element, and have that association remain stable for the lifetime of the element, or until the association definition is explicitly changed
- I as the author of a component might need to write a fully internal element association while also allowing external consumers of the component to write their own separate `id` associations into the component, sometimes even to the same element.
- Component consumers making `id` associations into a component should not need to be aware of or depend on a specific internal DOM structure. This has been a pain point in the past with styling, where authoring teams would write custom CSS selectors that would break on patch updates, and I wouldn't want to see that problem to leak over into element associations. I also have to admit to some amount of panic at the idea of our internal component DOM structure becoming effectively part of the public API (as it would be if consumers use it to create an internal association, as opposed to simply passing in an `id` string).
- Component consumers can often inject any custom DOM into specific areas of a component (i.e. like the idea of donut scoping without web components), and we want our internal `id` associations to not be affected by this.

Based on all that, I think trying to author element associations using CSS selectors that rely on a specific DOM relationship between two elements is inherently unstable over time in any sufficiently complex project.

If I had to choose between putting in extra work up front for more stable code, or being able to easily create a relationship that was prone to silently breaking, I would choose the first. This is also because accessibility especially tends to fail silently for most developers, not get tested, and remain uncaught for longer periods of time than other bugs.

On the other hand, I do very much agree that creating and passing around unique `id` strings across components is a pain point. The idea of defining something like scopes seems really promising though, as long as it would be possible to refer to the same element both using a scope (e.g. from within a component), and not using a scope (e.g. from outside the component).

I can’t see how a selectors-based design could improve robustness compared to the status quo, when:
- we're talking about a design which involves embedding a highly complex and tricky to master syntax inside string values inside an entirely different language, and 
- where the effects of getting the syntax wrong are largely invisible and subtle to debug.

I think the very best case scenario would be that it would allow some authors in some situations to write code which allowed them to avoid having to maintain matching strings in two locations in the DOM, which as @aardrian and @smhigley among others have already pointed out, are more likely than not to be _more_ fragile unless authors also take great pains not to depend on DOM structures or element properties which are subject to change. Even then, the robustness would be coming from those pains taken by authors, rather than from the feature design itself.

Moreover, even if those limited benefits were realised, the original problems with IDs would still remain in the cases where the selector-based API can't be used, either because authors aren't confident using the selector-based API, or because the DOM structure they're working with isn't amenable to writing selectors which don't depend on ID values.

Given the limited benefits and the significant implementation and ongoing maintenance work it would involve for browser engineers, and especially browser engineers on accessibility teams which are already  understaffed and overworked, I don't see how any selectors-based proposal is realistic.

Nevertheless, there are still several promising alternative avenues which have been raised already in this issue:

- Scoping has come up repeatedly, and as @bkardell points out seems to have a lot of potential for solving a large chunk of existing pain points.
- More generally, we've talked about the global namespace for IDs being a problem, which makes me wonder how far we could get with namespace-style scoping (i.e. you can refer to IDs in another scope, but only by prefixing them with the appropriate namespace; IDs in the same scope could be used unprefixed).
- Another type of scoping is per-attribute scoping, along the lines of @sorvell's [proposal using attribute-specific IDs](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10143#issuecomment-1974010952).
- @mayank had some interesting [suggestions for improving the DX of creating matching ID strings](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10143#issuecomment-2209641481).

If folks are still interested in working in this area, I'd personally really like to see a more comprehensive problem statement. Sarah's list above gives some critical requirements in addition to the very general points I summarised earlier from the top issue and the discussion, but it might be nice to spend some time collectively scoping out and documenting the existing pain points and requirements more systematically before we jump back into the weeds of discussing any particular solution.

Which brings me to my next point. I'm getting the sense that we've reached a bit of an impasse because we're discussing solutions without having consensus on use cases, so everyone has different use cases in mind.

Rather than jumping into solutions, perhaps it's easier to first reach consensus on what the main user needs are. In plain English, what would the author intent be? E.g. many if not most of my use cases are around getting the next/previous sibling, or the first sibling after/before that matches a given selector. These would not be doable with scoping, unless you insert a bunch of dummy grouping elements. Let's make this more concrete.

> Given the limited benefits and the significant implementation and ongoing maintenance work it would involve for browser engineers, and especially browser engineers on accessibility teams which are already understaffed and overworked, I don't see how any selectors-based proposal is realistic.

While ARIA is an incredibly significant use case, it's important not to lose sight of the big picture, or we could end up with a solution that is ergonomic for ARIA and little else. For example, the intent for ARIA references is much more frequently tightly scoped, whereas for things like popovers or `<datalist>` or invoker commands you have both tightly scoped use cases but also many cases where elements across an entire section or document even are referencing the same element. And let's not forget the extremely varied web component cases! This makes many scoping-based solutions tricky, e.g. you don't want to define a scope that applies to everything. Scoping is nice as an opt-in, but by itself it does not provide enough expressivity to really address the large variety of use cases. I think it's reasonable to prioritize ARIA use cases, but not to ignore everything else, to the point of referring to this as a purely a11y feature.

On that note, I'd suggest that folks re-read the OP. A lot of the solutions that are surfacing lately are things the OP had explored. Admittedly it got a bit in the weeds and it discussed solutions a bit too early (at the time people were not convinced that this is a problem worth solving, and by the time they were convinced, the conversation had moved away from the OP) but it could help save time.

I'm also wondering how much of the pushback against selectors is not based on their suitability to express author intent for element references, but because folks find them hard to read in general. If that's the case, diverging on an ad hoc basis is not likely to improve the web platform as a whole. To cite `<input pattern>` again, people generally find regular expressions even harder to read, but the benefit of referring to an existing established language (and benefitting from future improvements to it) outweighs any reasons for inventing a new syntax that is "easier" (at first at least — eventually the road all of these things end up going down is to need more power and then they end up developing a parallel syntax that is no longer simple AND lacks the consistency benefits).

I don't think that's true. `<input pattern>` is:
- a single attribute on a single element
- which uses a syntax designed for the purpose it's being used for, and
- breakages are (relatively) obvious and easily debugged.

Using selectors in order to set up associations between elements:
- applies to multiple attributes, many of which are global
- entails that these attributes all now have to support two different mechanisms of association, further complicating the syntax requirements
- uses a syntax which was designed and continues to be developed primarily for selecting _sets_ of elements for the purpose of styling, where
- breakages are, as you noted in your top comment, frequently invisible to most developers and users, and often subtle to debug.

I mention the original purpose of the syntax because the design constraints of selecting _sets_ of elements for the purposes of styling are at odds with those of designing a system for, as @smhigley [explained](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10143#issuecomment-3175870635), "identify[ing] exactly one other element, and have that association remain stable for the lifetime of the element, or until the association definition is explicitly changed." Yes, certain individual selectors allow you to select _exactly one_ element, but the _system_ of selectors as a whole is designed - brilliantly, it must be said - around the problem of styling similar elements in similar ways.

([Sarah's entire comment](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10143#issuecomment-3175870635) is highly worth re-reading: it contains a great deal of hard-won insight into the problems we're trying to solve here.)

@jcsteh [explained earlier](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10143#issuecomment-3154441665) what the burden would be specifically on browser accessibility engineers:

 "Gecko accessibility will need to query this whenever anything happens that could change the accessible name of an element. This will be difficult to do async because this needs to happen for every element on the page during the initial tree build, among other cases.
   
 "It will also need to be notified whenever any element is added to, removed from or mutated in the DOM such that the targets referenced by a selector change, plus it will need to map that back to the source element and attribute specifying the impacted selector. Upon being notified, it will need to query the selected targets."

It's probably not immediately obvious why that is a significant task, so I'll go into a bit more detail.

- Accessibility engines in browsers need to ensure that accessibility APIs are notified when certain changes occur in the accessibility tree, so that assistive technologies can maintain an accurate copy of the accessibility tree of the page, and potentially notify users of the change as well.
- This would be complex enough if it was only triggered by changes on the nodes themselves, but relationship attributes make this even more complex by introducing an "action at a distance" element.
- This is already true with IDs, and understanding why that is can help us understand why the situation would be even more complex with selectors.
  - Say you have `<input aria-describedby="help">`, and then another element is inserted into the DOM with an ID of `"help"`: that constitutes a change to the computed description of the input.
  - You could also change the ID of that newly inserted element which would then also change the description of the input, or you could insert an element earlier in the DOM with the same ID and different text content.
  - All of these cases need to be handled, so accessibility engines typically maintain a map of known ID back to the elements which refer to that ID (so, in this case, from `"help"` to the `<input>`). Then, when certain DOM updates occur, such as an ID attribute change or an element insertion, this "reverse relation" map can be used to update the impacted element(s) as appropriate - in this instance, changing the computed description of the `<input>` and firing the necessary tree update events for assistive technology to consume.
- To make this work with selectors, we would instead need a way to be notified whenever, as Jamie says, "whenever any element is added to, removed from or mutated in the DOM such that the targets referenced by a selector change" and likewise map that back to the referring element.
    - This is all technically achievable with enough effort, but the most likely outcome is that this code would be live in the accessibility engine for the same reason that the "reverse ID mapping" code does: the accessibility engine is the only consumer for these types of updates. Other consumers for ID mappings can get by with just computing the _forward_ mapping on an ad-hoc basis (e.g. on `click`, or in an IDL attribute getter, although there are additional challenges there around performance and staleness).
    - Even if engineers on other teams assisted with the initial implementation of this logic, the team that owns the code would have to take on the burden of advising on its integration, reviewing the code, and then maintaining it once the original authors have moved on to other projects.

> While ARIA is an incredibly significant use case, it's important not to lose sight of the big picture, or we could end up with a solution that is ergonomic for ARIA and little else. For example, the intent for ARIA references is much more frequently tightly scoped, whereas for things like popovers or `<datalist>` or invoker commands you have both tightly scoped use cases but also many cases where elements across an entire section or document even are referencing the same element. 
    
It's simply not the case in any way that ARIA references tend to be more tightly scoped. In fact:
- `popovertarget` is [mapped](https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aam-1.0/#att-popovertarget) to [`aria-details`](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria/#aria-details)
- `list` is [mapped](https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aam-1.0/#att-list) to [`aria-controls`](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria/#aria-controls)
- `commandfor` is also [mapped](https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aam-1.0/#att-command-popovers)  to `aria-details`.

In other words, a solution designed to work for `aria-details` and `aria-controls` would automatically also work for `popovertarget`, `list` and `commandfor`, since they are fundamentally expressing analogous relationships and will tend to be used in analogous ways.

We're at no risk of losing sight of the big picture by benefiting from the expertise of developers with experience using ARIA attributes, since without exception those developers also use HTML attributes (it's a [tenet of ARIA usage](https://www.w3.org/TR/using-aria/#rule1) that HTML features be used _in preference_ to ARIA features where possible). Moreover, accessibility specialists like @smhigley and @scottaohara have contributed significantly to the design of new HTML features like `popovertarget`.

We're at no risk of designing a feature which works well for ARIA features but not for other HTML features, since the purpose of ARIA is to describe user interfaces: ARIA relationship attributes exist to describe relationships that are meaningful in user interfaces, just like HTML attributes do, so they cover a very similar conceptual space.

We are at risk, though, of missing an opportunity to design something that actually could help developers with the pain points of using IDs.

I believe [htmx](https://htmx.org/) is a good library to look at. It has support for the following targets ([docs](https://htmx.org/docs/#targets)):

  > `hx-target`, and most attributes that take a CSS selector, support an “extended” CSS syntax:
  >

  > - The `closest <CSS selector>` syntax will find the [closest](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Element/closest) ancestor element or itself, that matches the given CSS selector. (e.g. closest tr will target the closest table row to the element)
  > - The `next <CSS selector>` syntax will find the next element in the DOM matching the given CSS selector.
  > - The `previous <CSS selector>` syntax will find the previous element in the DOM matching the given CSS selector.
